name: Reloxin

lead: Reloxin was the name used in the United States for abobotulinumtoxinA, a botulinum toxin type A product made by Ipsen and marketed by Medicis, now sold as Dysport (Azzalure in Europe for cosmetic use). It is injected into facial muscles to soften lines, especially the frown lines between the eyebrows.
The appearance payoff is a smoother, less furrowed upper face. Trials showed significantly more people improving than with placebo, with effects lasting a few months.

paras: A clinician injects small amounts into specific muscles; smoothing typically appears within days and peaks about a week later, then fades over roughly two to four months, so treatment is repeated. Details of dosing are set by the prescriber.

Reported effects include injection-site reactions, headache, and, in the long-term study, nervous-system-related events; spread of toxin beyond the injection site can cause weakness elsewhere, and the FDA added boxed warnings in 2009. It is prescription-only.

chain: Smoother forehead and glabella for months
angle.text: Reloxin/Dysport is injected to soften frown lines by temporarily relaxing the muscles that crease the skin. Results appear within days and last a few months.

lead: Reloxin was the proposed United States brand name for abobotulinumtoxinA, the botulinum toxin type A made by Ipsen and sold elsewhere as Dysport and for cosmetic use in Europe as Azzalure. A 2012 review lists Dysport, Azzalure and Reloxin together as the same product [1].

Cosmetically, it is used to reduce frown lines (glabellar lines) by relaxing the underlying muscles, producing a smoother upper face. Reviews describe it as effective and well tolerated for facial aesthetic use [1]. A 2009 open-label study followed 1,200 patients given up to five treatments over 13 months [2].
In 2009 the FDA renamed several botulinum toxins to stress they are not interchangeable and retained abobotulinumtoxinA as the generic name for Dysport [3].
infobox: Ipsen; Medicis in the early US trials

paras: The cosmetic use is treatment of moderate to severe glabellar lines [2][4]. Botulinum toxins generally are used on the upper third of the face; smoothing is usually visible in three to five days and lasts two to four months [3]. Newer techniques aim for natural results rather than a frozen look, and interest from men is increasing [1].

A randomized, placebo-controlled study tested 20, 50 and 75 U doses; each produced significantly more responders than placebo, and the 50 U dose was reported as effective as 75 U with similar duration [4]. A randomized double-blind study compared Botox and Dysport/Reloxin on forehead wrinkles and muscle electrical activity [5].

In the 13-month safety study, most adverse events were judged unlikely to be related to treatment, and related events occurred in 36% of patients, most commonly injection-site disorders (18%) [2]. In the dose study, headache and nasopharyngitis were most common and similar across groups [4]. Toxin spread can cause weakness in other muscles, and the FDA added boxed warnings in 2009 [3].
The name Reloxin was used by Medicis in the US phase III program [2]. In 2009 the FDA renamed botulinum toxin products to emphasize they are not interchangeable [3].

A phase III long-term study of 1,200 patients treated for glabellar lines with up to five treatments assessed safety over 13 months [2]. A dose-ranging trial found significant improvement over placebo at 20, 50 and 75 U [4]. A comparative trial examined Botox versus Dysport/Reloxin on forehead lines [5]. A 2012 review summarizes progress in facial esthetic use [1].

timeline.event: Randomized dose-ranging trial of Reloxin for glabellar lines published [4].
